migrationNotes: Spine: judge an argument with two separate inspections, first the join between premises and conclusion (cases, then counterexamples), then the premises themselves, and finally put the two together as soundness.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): valid-but-untrue-hook, valid-but-untrue-2.

lesson.title: Valid but untrue

lead.text: Go back to the dragon story and ask the two questions separately. The first is whether the claims are true, and they aren't, since nobody owns a dragon. The second is whether the conclusion would have to be true if the premises were. Here the answer is yes. If every dragon owner is rich and Ana owns a dragon, then Ana is rich, and there is no way to keep the premises and deny the conclusion.

The second question is about the link between the claims, and logic has a word for an argument that passes it. An argument is valid when there is no case in which all its premises are true and its conclusion is false. A case here means a way things could be, like a row of a truth table, and it does not have to be a way things actually are. So validity says nothing about whether the premises hold in the real world.

People often use “valid” to mean “true” or “sensible”, and it means neither. A valid argument is a guarantee about a connection: give it true premises and a true conclusion comes out. It does not supply the true premises.
Think about the guarantee a valid argument gives, and about what it is a guarantee of.

steps.headline: Testing a pattern against the cases

lead.text: Real arguments carry details that have nothing to do with the link, so we test the shape instead, using letters. Take “Lamp 1 is on and lamp 2 is on, so lamp 2 is on.” With p for the first claim and q for the second, it becomes “p ∧ q; therefore q”. A semicolon separates the premises, and here there is only one.

To test a shape, look through the four rows for a bad one. Each row is a possible case, and a bad row is one where every premise is true and the conclusion is false. Only the row TT makes p ∧ q true, and q is true in it. Every other row has a false premise, so none of them can be bad. No bad row exists, so the pattern is valid.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the search skipped every row where a premise was false. Those rows promise nothing, because validity only speaks about cases in which the premises hold. To test a pattern, find the rows where all the premises hold, then check the conclusion in those rows.

lead.text: Test “p → q; p; therefore q” against the four rows. You are looking for a row where both premises are true and q is false.

reveal.text: Compare your answer with the rows. Wherever p → q and p are both true, q is true as well.

steps.headline: A bad row has a name

lead.text: Not every pattern passes the test. Try “p; therefore p ∧ q”, which says that because one lamp is on, both are. The rows where the premise p holds are TT and TF. In TT the conclusion p ∧ q is true, but in TF it is false, so the premise holds and the conclusion fails.

A case like TF has a name. A counterexample to an argument is a case that makes every premise true and the conclusion false. It is the one thing a valid argument cannot have, so validity can be put another way: a valid argument has no counterexamples.
Finding a counterexample is how you show that an argument is invalid. The next example does exactly that, one row at a time.

steps.headline: Is “p ∨ q; q; therefore p” valid?

lead.text: Keep only the rows where every premise is true, and compare the conclusion with each.

workedSteps.text: Look for a row where both premises are true.
In FT, p ∨ q and q are true, but the conclusion p is false.
A counterexample exists, so the argument is not valid.

lead.text: Look for a counterexample to this pattern: a row where both premises hold and the conclusion p fails.

steps.headline: Valid is not the same as true

lead.text: A valid argument can still go wrong, because validity checks the link and leaves the facts alone. The dragon story has a valid link and a false first premise. So does this one: “Every even number is divisible by 4. The number 8 is even. So 8 is divisible by 4.” The first premise is false, since 6 is even and 6 is not divisible by 4. The conclusion is true all the same.

That shows what validity can't do. A valid argument that starts from a false premise gives you no reason to believe its conclusion. Sometimes the conclusion is false, and sometimes, as with the number 8, it comes out true by luck. An argument earns your trust only when both checks pass. A valid argument whose premises are all true is called sound. An argument that fails either check is unsound, and a sound argument always has a true conclusion, because the link carries the truth across.

So the two inspections stay separate. Logic does the first by looking at cases. The second inspection asks whether the premises are true. That is a matter for evidence, and each premise has to be checked on its own.
Soundness asks for two things. Here the argument is described by what it passes and fails, so decide which check it fails.
A learner is judging an argument whose conclusion is plainly false, and blames the reasoning.

lesson.orientation: Judge whether a conclusion follows separately from whether the premises are true.
lesson.nextAction: Recognise that a conclusion can follow from false premises.

blocks.text: A flatmate reads a line from a story aloud: “Everyone who owns a dragon is rich. Ana owns a dragon. So Ana is rich.” The other flatmate groans. “That can't be right. There are no dragons.”

She has a point about the dragons, and yet something in the line holds. Suppose the story were true and a dragon really did sit in Ana's garden. Then the money would follow, and nobody could sensibly say Ana was poor. Two questions have got tangled: whether the story is true, and whether the money follows from it. Plenty of disagreements stall because people answer one when they were asked the other.

This lesson pulls the two questions apart. It builds a way of testing whether one claim follows from others without knowing whether those claims are true, using the rows of the table from earlier. It ends by putting the two tests back together.

intro.promise: By the end you'll judge whether an argument is valid from the cases alone, and say when a valid argument is still unsound.

recap.keyIdea: An argument is valid when no case makes the premises true and the conclusion false. It is sound only if it is valid and its premises are true.

blocks.text: You separated the dragon story's link from its facts, and tested patterns by looking for a row where the premises hold and the conclusion fails. That search found a counterexample to “p → q; q; therefore p”, in the row with p false and q true.

recap.nextHook: Some invalid patterns look valid because they resemble one that works. The next lesson starts from a wet street and names the commonest ways of misusing an if-then rule.

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p → q; p; therefore q” valid or invalid?
hints: Ask whether both premises can be true while q is false.
The first premise links p to q, and the second states p.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No row makes both premises true and q false.

questions.onCorrect: Valid. In every row where both premises hold, q holds too.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where both premises are true and q is false. Is there one?

questions.prompt: How many counterexamples may a valid argument have?
hints: Validity says no case has true premises and a false conclusion.
What does the definition allow for such cases?
Count the exceptions it permits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A single counterexample would make it invalid, so a valid argument has none.

questions.onCorrect: None. One counterexample would make the argument invalid.

misconceptions.feedback: One counterexample is enough to make an argument invalid. How many does validity permit?
Validity is a guarantee over every case. How many exceptions does that allow?

questions.prompt: Is the argument “p → q; q; therefore p” valid or invalid?
hints: Look for a row where p → q and q are both true.
Of those rows, check whether the conclusion p is true in every one.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The false–true row is a counterexample.

questions.onCorrect: Invalid. With p false and q true, both premises hold and the conclusion fails.

misconceptions.feedback: Test the row with p false and q true. Do both premises hold, and what happens to p?

questions.prompt: A valid argument contains a false premise. Is it sound or unsound?
hints: Soundness needs two things: validity and true premises.
Does the stated premise meet the second?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Soundness requires validity and all true premises.

questions.onCorrect: Unsound. Soundness needs every premise to be true as well as validity.

misconceptions.feedback: Validity alone isn't enough. What does soundness also ask of the premises?

questions.prompt: A valid argument has all true premises. Is it sound or unsound?
hints: Recall both parts of the definition of soundness.
The question gives you validity and true premises.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It meets both requirements for soundness.

questions.onCorrect: Sound. It is valid and every premise is true.

misconceptions.feedback: Soundness needs validity and true premises. Does this argument have both?

questions.prompt: How many true-premise, false-conclusion cases are needed to refute validity?
hints: Validity says there are no cases with true premises and a false conclusion.
One exception breaks a promise about every case.
You don't need most of the table to be counterexamples.
questions.onCorrect: One. A single case with true premises and a false conclusion refutes validity.

misconceptions.feedback: With no such case, the argument is valid. How many are needed to refute it?
You don't need several. Validity promises there are none.

questions.prompt: If the first two sentences were true, would Ana have to be rich? Answer yes or no.
hints: Imagine the first two sentences are true. What follows about Ana?
Ignore whether dragons exist.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. A dragon owner is rich, and Ana owns one.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. If the premises held, Ana would have to be rich. Whether they hold is a separate question.

misconceptions.feedback: Suppose the first two sentences are true, whatever the real world is like. Could Ana avoid being rich?

questions.prompt: All the premises of a valid argument are true. Must its conclusion be true? Answer yes or no.
hints: Is there any case with true premises and a false conclusion?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. A valid argument has no case with true premises and a false conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. Validity rules out true premises with a false conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: A valid argument has no case with true premises and a false conclusion. What does that leave?

questions.prompt: Why is one counterexample enough to show an argument invalid?
hints: What does validity promise about cases?

acceptedIdeas: Validity promises there is no such case, and one case breaks the promise.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Validity promises no case with true premises and a false conclusion. One is enough to break it.

questions.onCorrect: Validity is a promise about every case, so a single exception breaks it.

choices.label: Validity promises there is no such case, and one case breaks the promise.
Most of the rows have to be counterexamples.
The premises are false in all the other rows.

misconceptions.feedback: Validity allows no such case at all. It is not a matter of how many.
The other rows don't matter. Validity is about cases with true premises.

questions.prompt: “All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. So penguins can fly.” A learner says: “It's invalid, because the conclusion is false.” Is the learner right? Answer yes or no.
hints: Imagine the premises are true. Could the conclusion still be false?
Is a false conclusion the same as an invalid argument?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. If the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be. The argument is valid but unsound.

questions.onCorrect: No. The conclusion follows from the premises, so it is valid. The first premise is false, so it is unsound.

misconceptions.feedback: A false conclusion doesn't make an argument invalid. Ask whether true premises would force it.

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p ∨ q; ¬p; therefore q” valid or invalid?
hints: Find the rows where both premises are true.
Is q true in every one of them?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the row with p false and q true keeps both premises true, and q is true there.

questions.onCorrect: Valid. The only row where both premises hold is FT, and q is true there.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where p ∨ q and ¬p are both true and q is false. Is there one?
